stops.name: Gray's Inn — the Essays, and the Walks planted
stops.campa: Bacon publishes the first slim Essays, ten of them, terse counsel on studies, discourse, honor, and negotiation, the beginning of a book he will keep enlarging the rest of his life. The same year he takes the Gray's Inn garden in hand, laying out the Walks with elms and raised mounts, a design so lasting that Londoners still stroll it centuries on. Words for the mind and trees for the eye, planted in the same season: already the man who will one day found Salomon's House, tending letters and gardens both as forms of one instauration.

stops.name: London — arrested for debt
stops.campa: Bacon's debts catch up with him: on the twenty-third of September he is arrested for debt and held, not long, in a sponging house in the City, an embarrassment to a rising counsel and Queen's servant. Essex, ever generous where his own fortunes allow, helps settle the matter, deepening still further the weight of favor Bacon owes him. The man who will one day hold the Great Seal of England cannot yet keep his own accounts in order, a fault that will follow him, in one form or another, to the very end of his public life.

stops.name: Essex House — the Rebellion
stops.campa: Robert Devereux, ruined in fortune and standing after his failed Irish command, gathers armed followers at Essex House and marches them into the City, hoping to raise the citizens against the councillors he blames for his fall. The City does not rise. Within hours the rebellion collapses and Essex surrenders. Bacon, who has warned his friend and patron for years against exactly this kind of rashness, and who has already begun distancing himself in letters to Robert Cecil, watches the ruin of a man he owes almost everything, from across a widening gulf.

stops.name: Westminster Hall — the trial
stops.campa: At the trial in Westminster Hall, Bacon stands among the Crown's counsel prosecuting the earl who made his career possible, arguing treason against the friend who gave him Twickenham Park and every start he never got from the Queen. It is the disagreeable task, discharged, contemporaries will say, with more zeal than the office strictly required. Essex and Southampton are convicted; only Essex is condemned to die. Bacon's own voice helped seal it, and the fact will follow him into every account he writes of his own life hereafter.

stops.name: The Tower of London — the execution
stops.campa: On the green within the Tower, spared the crowd of Tower Hill by the Queen's own mercy, Robert Devereux is beheaded, still protesting his loyalty to her person even as he dies a traitor to her state. Bacon does not attend, but will spend the rest of his life answering for the part he played in bringing the earl here: counselor turned prosecutor, friend who chose the Crown. Elizabeth herself, it is said, never fully recovers her old brightness after this execution; within two years she too will be dead.

stops.name: London — the Apologie published
stops.campa: Three years on, with a new king on the throne and old wounds unhealed, Bacon publishes his Apologie, in Certaine Imputations Concerning the Late Earle of Essex: a careful, self-justifying account of every service and every warning given his fallen patron, and of why the prosecution was duty and not betrayal. It persuades some and not others. The charge of ingratitude will be repeated against him for the rest of his career and long after, a shadow not even the Novum Organum will fully dispel.

stops.name: Whitehall — knighted by the new king
stops.campa: With the accession of James VI of Scotland as James I of England, three hundred gentlemen are knighted in a single sweeping ceremony to mark the new reign, and Bacon is one of them, his old service to Elizabeth's Essex now safely behind a king who owes him nothing and everything is still to be won. He sets himself at once to court the new sovereign's favor with treatises and flattery both, reading in James's own pedantic learning an opening no other client at court can match.

stops.name: London — The Advancement of Learning published
stops.campa: Bacon publishes The Advancement of Learning, dedicated to King James: a survey of the whole map of human knowledge and of everywhere it has been neglected, corrupted, or falsely finished before its time. It is the first public sketch of the project that will occupy the rest of his life, not a single book of philosophy but an instauration, a rebuilding of learning from its foundations, so knowledge might finally bear fruit for the relief of man's estate rather than merely furnish disputation for the schools.

stops.name: Marylebone Chapel — marriage to Alice Barnham
stops.campa: At Marylebone Chapel, in the fields north of London, Bacon marries Alice Barnham, daughter of a London alderman and not yet fourteen. He comes clad from top to toe in purple, and the cloth of silver and gold he orders for them both draws so deep into her portion that the court letter-writers make a joke of it. It is a marriage of property and connection more than passion. The couple will have no children, and in a will drawn in bitterness in 1625 Bacon will revoke every gift and settlement made to her, leaving her, in his own cold phrase, to her right only.

stops.name: Westminster — Solicitor General
stops.campa: After a decade of disappointed applications under Elizabeth, Bacon is at last appointed Solicitor General, the office he had twice failed to win before, now granted under a king more susceptible to his particular blend of learning, flattery, and legal craft. It is the true beginning of the second half of his career: the climb through the great offices of the Crown that will carry him, within little more than a decade, to the highest civil office in the land, and not much later, to the fastest fall of any Lord Chancellor in English history.

stops.name: Westminster — Attorney General
stops.campa: Bacon is made Attorney General, the Crown's chief law officer, a post he pursues with the same patient ambition brought to every rung below it. He is now the most powerful lawyer in England after the judges themselves, and will use the place to draw closer still to the king's favorites, first Somerset and then the young Buckingham, whose rise he helps engineer and whose favor will carry him, in turn, to the woolsack.

stops.name: Kassel — the Fama Fraternitatis circulates
stops.campa: In the German lands, a strange manifesto begins to circulate in manuscript and then in print at Kassel: the Fama Fraternitatis, announcing to all Europe a hidden brotherhood of the Rosy Cross, founded generations before by one Christian Rosenkreuz, keepers of a secret natural philosophy and a promise of universal reformation. A persistent tradition, never proved and never quite silenced, holds that the guiding hand, even the pen, behind the Rosicrucian manifestos was Bacon's own, working through continental intermediaries to seed abroad the same instauration he was building at home in English.
